metadata.title: The correspondence between PISA performance and school achievement in Finland

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses Finnish PISA 2015 and PISA 2018 microdata with a two-stage sampling design. For analyses that include PISA achievement, the authors state that student final weights and 80 replicate weights are required to compute standard errors, following OECD guidance. The descriptive table note indicates that reported percentages and means are weighted values, implying that sampling weights were applied in at least the descriptive statistics and likely in the inferential analyses. The manuscript does not name the specific weight variable codes (e.g., W_FSTUWT), so the exact weight variable name cannot be extracted, but the intended complex-survey approach is clearly documented.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper reports that PISA proficiency scores/levels are used and that plausible values (10 PVs) are handled by performing analyses for each PV and aggregating results, but it does not describe any additional missing-data procedure for the linked register outcomes or background variables. This is a reporting gap because missingness handling can affect regression estimates and standard errors, especially when linking PISA to external register data. The authors’ focus is on PV methodology and complex survey weights, leaving missing-data treatment unspecified.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used Finnish PISA 2015 and PISA 2018 data linked to national register education records containing end-of-basic-education grades. Included only Finnish 15-year-old PISA participants who were in grade 9 and who applied to upper secondary education through the joint application system in the spring of their PISA participation. Excluded the PISA 2018 financial literacy option subsample (n=1954). Excluded students tested in Swedish from the main analysis implicitly by using the grade linkage for the Finnish basic sample (the paper reports Swedish-tested shares but does not state a separate analytic restriction beyond the grade-9/joint-application linkage).

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 (Finland) Grade 9 Reading proficiency level → mother tongue & literature grade
main_findings.target_variable: Mother tongue & literature grade (predicted by PISA reading level)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported (regression coefficients/SEs in Table 3 are not fully present in the provided text; correlations reported elsewhere: r≈0.58 for PISA reading scores with mother tongue & literature grade).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 (Finland) Grade 9 the study leveraged PISA reading proficiency level (and, in the adjusted model, gender and ESCS) to predict mother tongue & literature grades, finding that higher PISA proficiency levels correspond to higher school grades. This indicates that PISA reading performance has meaningful predictive validity for Finnish end-of-basic-education grading, supporting the use of PISA results as an informative indicator for school achievement patterns, though the study is correlational/associational rather than causal.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 (Finland) Grade 9 Mathematics proficiency level → mathematics grade
main_findings.target_variable: Mathematics grade (predicted by PISA mathematics level)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported for regression (Table 3 coefficients not fully shown in provided text); correlations reported: r≈0.58 for PISA mathematics scores with mathematics grade.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 (Finland) Grade 9 the study leveraged PISA mathematics proficiency level (and, in the adjusted model, gender and ESCS) to predict mathematics grades, finding that PISA proficiency levels predict grades in mathematics. This indicates that PISA mathematics results align with Finnish school grading outcomes, suggesting that system-level monitoring using PISA can reflect classroom-level achievement differences, while causality cannot be inferred from the regression framework used.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 (Finland) Grade 9 Science proficiency level → science-related grades (mean of physics/chemistry/biology/geography)
main_findings.target_variable: Science-related grades (predicted by PISA science level)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported for regression (Table 3 coefficients not fully shown in provided text); correlations reported: highest r≈0.66 between PISA science scores and science-related grades in PISA 2015.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 (Finland) Grade 9 the study leveraged PISA science proficiency level (and, in the adjusted model, gender and ESCS) to predict science-related grades, finding a strong positive correspondence between PISA science performance and Finnish science-related school grades. This indicates that PISA science can serve as a useful proxy for end-of-basic-education science achievement patterns, though the linkage may be influenced by how grades incorporate both achievement and non-cognitive factors.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 (Finland) Grade 9 Reading proficiency level → mother tongue & literature grade
main_findings.target_variable: Mother tongue & literature grade (predicted by PISA reading level)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported for regression (Table 3 coefficients not fully shown in provided text); correlations reported: r≈0.62 for PISA reading scores with mother tongue & literature grade.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 (Finland) Grade 9 the study leveraged PISA reading proficiency level (and, in the adjusted model, gender and ESCS) to predict mother tongue & literature grades, finding that higher PISA reading levels are associated with higher school grades. This indicates that the relationship between PISA reading performance and Finnish grading is stable across PISA cycles, supporting longitudinal interpretation of PISA trends for school achievement monitoring.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 (Finland) Grade 9 Mathematics proficiency level → mathematics grade
main_findings.target_variable: Mathematics grade (predicted by PISA mathematics level)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported for regression (Table 3 coefficients not fully shown in provided text); correlations reported: r≈0.58 for PISA mathematics scores with mathematics grade.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 (Finland) Grade 9 the study leveraged PISA mathematics proficiency level (and, in the adjusted model, gender and ESCS) to predict mathematics grades, finding that PISA mathematics proficiency levels predict mathematics grades. This indicates that PISA mathematics performance reflects Finnish school achievement in mathematics, but the study’s reliance on linked grades means results may also capture grading practices and non-cognitive influences.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 (Finland) Grade 9 Science proficiency level → science-related grades (mean of physics/chemistry/biology/geography)
main_findings.target_variable: Science-related grades (predicted by PISA science level)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported for regression (Table 3 coefficients not fully shown in provided text); correlations reported: r≈0.63 between PISA science scores and science-related grades in PISA 2018.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 (Finland) Grade 9 the study leveraged PISA science proficiency level (and, in the adjusted model, gender and ESCS) to predict science-related grades, finding a positive correspondence between PISA science performance and Finnish science-related school grades. This indicates that PISA science results can inform expectations about school achievement in science, while caution is needed because PV estimation may not account for the linked register information used to form the outcome.

data.outcome_summary: The study links Finnish PISA 2015 and PISA 2018 (grade 9, ages 15) to national register grades from end-of-basic-education certificates, using PISA proficiency levels in reading, mathematics, and science as predictors of corresponding subject grades. It first reports Pearson correlations between PISA proficiency scores and grades, finding correlations around 0.60 across domains (e.g., up to r=0.66 for science-related grades in 2015) and also non-corresponding grade correlations, suggesting limited discriminant validity. It then estimates ordinary least-squares regressions separately for each domain, using PISA proficiency levels (Model 1) and adding gender and ESCS (Model 2), concluding that PISA levels predict grades even after controlling for SES. The analysis uses PISA complex survey design with student final weights and 80 replicate weights and handles 10 plausible values by running analyses for each PV and aggregating. A key limitation is that linking external register data may bias PV-based estimates because PV estimation does not incorporate the added information, so results should be interpreted as predictive/associational rather than causal.
